paragraphs.heading: A score for how well a model fits
paragraphs.text: The coefficient of determination, written R² and read as R squared, tells you what share of the variation in an outcome can be predicted from the variables used to explain it. It measures how closely a model reproduces the outcomes that were actually observed. In short, it is a measure of goodness of fit. It is used both for models built to predict and for models built to test hypotheses.

paragraphs.heading: The ends of the scale
paragraphs.text: If the model's values match every observed value exactly, R² equals 1. A baseline model that always predicts the mean of the observed data scores R² of 0. Because R² can be stated as a percentage, it can be easier to read than error measures such as MSE or RMSE, whose ranges are arbitrary.

paragraphs.heading: Link to correlation
paragraphs.text: In simple linear regression with an intercept, r² is just the square of the sample correlation coefficient r. When further predictors are added, R² becomes the squared coefficient of multiple correlation. In both of these cases it is always below 1 and usually above 0. Several different definitions of R² exist, and they only sometimes agree.

paragraphs.heading: When R² goes negative
paragraphs.text: R² can drop below zero. This can happen when the predictions were not produced by fitting a model to those same data. It can also happen after fitting, for example in a linear regression with no intercept or when a nonlinear function is fitted. A negative value means that simply using the mean of the data would fit the outcomes better than the model does.

paragraphs.heading: Why more variables mislead
paragraphs.text: When a model is fitted by ordinary least squares, R² never falls as you add variables; it can only stay level or rise. That invites a bad habit of piling in variables just to push R² up. Suppose you predict a car's sales from its mileage, price and engine power. You could add the first letter of its name or the height of its lead engineer, and R² would not drop and would likely creep up by chance alone.

paragraphs.heading: The adjusted version
paragraphs.text: This problem leads to a second measure, adjusted R². It is read in nearly the same way as R², but it is penalized as extra variables enter the model. R² values can be worked out for any kind of predictive model, even one with no statistical basis.
